_readme: 50 long-tail search terms for the North American specification market, with the page
that should own each one and an honest note on whether we can serve it today.
WHERE THESE COME FROM, AND WHERE THEY DO NOT.
They are NOT the output of asking a model to invent fifty plausible phrases. That
method was proposed on 2026-09-09 and declined for a specific reason: we already have
44 countries of observed query data from Search Console and Bing, and replacing
measured demand with guesses is a downgrade. See the note in
docs/collaboration/2026-09-10-gtm-north-america.md, section 8, item 7.
What we DID lack is the North American trade vocabulary, and that gap is real: a buyer
arrived on 2026-09-09 carrying the competitor part number `rxfse25r510l32d3`, whose
`32D` fragment is a US finish code. Our catalogue answers in house codes. So these
terms are drawn from three evidenced sources:
observed   a query we have actually seen, or a fragment of a real buyer's part number
trade      vocabulary verified on the sites the client named — Trudoor's own category
structure, Precision's Apex 2000 catalogue, I Dig Hardware's code articles,
and the published ANSI/BHMA A156.3 and A156.18 standards
catalogue  a model, dimension or feature our own records already state
`canServe` is the column that matters and it is deliberately harsh:
yes       the page can answer this today, truthfully
partial   we can answer for some models but not the range
no        we cannot answer it honestly yet, and the blocker is named
A term marked `no` must NOT be targeted with copy until its blocker clears. Ranking
for `grade 1 panic bar` while holding no ANSI certification wins a click and loses the
buyer at the submittal, which is worse than not ranking.
Report: node scripts/build-longtail-report.mjs
